passage:
"Santosh, did you hear about Farida from accounts?"
"Only that she was called to HR on Monday."
"That's not what the floor group says. They say money went missing."
"Who said that?"
"Someone from sales. And the canteen group says police came."
"Police? I was here all Monday, Indu. No police came."
"Now the third floor thinks she's already fired."
"Hang on. Monday: HR meeting. Tuesday: money. Today: police and fired. It gets bigger every floor."
"She ate lunch alone today. Nobody sat with her."
"Did anyone ask her? Or HR? Or the person who said it first?"
"...I don't even know who said it first."
"Neither does anyone. Come on."
"Where?"
"To sit with her at lunch. And if anyone asks us, we say what we actually know: she had a meeting."
Farida looked up, surprised, when they pulled out the chairs.

qa.q: What did the canteen group say had happened?
qa.a: The canteen group said police came.

qa.q: How does Santosh seem to feel as the story keeps growing?
qa.a: Santosh is uneasy and doubtful, having been there all Monday and knowing no police came, so the story is clearly swelling without facts.

qa.q: What small step do Santosh and Indu take to stop the rumour's harm?
qa.a: They sit with Farida at lunch and agree to repeat only what they know, that she had a meeting, instead of passing the story on.

qa.q: What is it like for Farida while the rumour moves between floors?
qa.a: Farida is left eating lunch alone, judged by people who never asked her, and her surprise at company shows how isolated she had become.

grounding: Santosh and Indu watch a rumour about Farida from accounts grow from a meeting into theft and firing as it passes between groups, harming her before anyone checks.

passage:
I watched a rumour nearly cost Suraj his job last winter.
Suraj has been the night watchman in our building for six years. One morning a cycle went missing from the basement. In the Block A group someone wrote, "Watchman was asleep." In Block B it became, "Watchman must know something." By evening the combined group said, "Suraj sold it, obviously," and three people asked the society to change the security agency.
I kept reading the messages and waiting for someone to ask who saw anything. Nobody did. I didn't either, for two whole days.
On the third day, the cycle's owner found it at the repair shop on Station Road. His son had left it there for a puncture.
There was one short message: "Cycle found." No apology.
Suraj still greets everyone at the gate. He doesn't smile at Block A the way he used to.
Deepak

qa.q: Where was the missing cycle found?
qa.a: The cycle was found at the repair shop on Station Road.

qa.q: What does Deepak's admission "I didn't either, for two whole days" suggest Deepak feels now?
qa.a: It suggests Deepak feels regret and some guilt for staying silent while the story grew, even while seeing that nobody had asked for evidence.

qa.q: What could someone in the groups have done on the first morning?
qa.a: Someone could have asked who actually saw anything, or spoken to Suraj and the cycle's owner, before the guesses turned into an accusation.

qa.q: How has the rumour affected Suraj, even after the cycle was found?
qa.a: Suraj still does his job, but he no longer smiles at Block A the way he used to, because he was accused without evidence and never received an apology.

grounding: Deepak watches a rumour about a building watchman grow from group to group into an accusation, doing harm before anyone asks who started it.

passage:
Supervisor's log, stitching unit, Friday. Seema
Monday: in the morning shift, someone said Bhavna from finishing "was seen talking long with the owner's son".
Tuesday: the afternoon-shift version was that Bhavna "is getting promoted because of him".
Wednesday: by the night shift it had become that Bhavna "takes money" and "reports on all of us". Two women moved their chairs away from her at lunch. Bhavna ate alone, eyes on her phone, and left early. I felt sick watching it.
Nobody I asked knew who first said it. Everyone had "heard".
What I did: on Thursday I asked Bhavna privately. The owner's son had been sorting out her late overtime pay, which I had flagged myself. I told her I was sorry it had gone this far. Today I spoke to each shift with the facts and asked that we check before we repeat. I also asked HR to note it.

qa.q: What was the Monday version of the rumour?
qa.a: That Bhavna from finishing 'was seen talking long with the owner's son'.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling as the story grew, and what shows it?
qa.a: Seema felt sick watching Bhavna eat alone, especially since nobody could say who first started the story.

qa.q: What steps did Seema take, and why do they help?
qa.a: Asking Bhavna privately, learning the real reason, then giving each shift the facts and asking HR to note it, so the story stopped growing.

qa.q: What was that week like for Bhavna?
qa.a: Bhavna went from being noticed to being shunned, eating alone and leaving early, harmed before anyone asked who first said it.

grounding: Shows a supervisor watching a rumour about a worker grow shift by shift, and the harm done before anyone traced its source.

passage:
Wednesday
Watched a rumour grow legs this week and did nothing until today.
Sunday, in the morning walkers' group: "New tenants in B-702 get visitors late at night."
Monday, in the parents' group: "Something shady going on in B-702, keep kids away."
Tuesday the security guard told me, very seriously, that "the police came" to B-702. They didn't. I was home all evening.
Today in the lift I met Swati from B-702 with a tiffin carrier. She works night shifts at the hospital. The "visitors" are colleagues who drop her home at 2 am. She said the watchman had stopped smiling at her and a mother had pulled her child away in the park. She said it lightly. Her hands weren't light.
Tonight I posted what I knew in all three groups, and asked whoever started it to say where it came from. Silence so far.
Chinmay

qa.q: What does Swati do for work?
qa.a: Swati works night shifts at the hospital.

qa.q: How does Chinmay feel about the week, and what shows it?
qa.a: Chinmay feels guilty about staying silent; the entry opens by admitting doing nothing until today and ends with posting the facts.

qa.q: What did Chinmay do that others in the society could copy?
qa.a: Posted the known facts in every group where the rumour had spread and asked whoever started it to say where it came from.

qa.q: What is it like for Swati living under the rumour?
qa.a: Swati is treated as suspicious by the watchman and a mother in the park; she speaks lightly, but her hands show how much it hurts.

grounding: Shows a neighbour watching a rumour about new tenants grow across society groups and harm her before anyone asked for its source.

Chandrika: yesterday it was "someone had an upset stomach". today it's old meat
Sharmila: well someone must know
Chandrika: who first said it?

Chandrika: asked Meenu. she heard it in the lift. the lift doesn't talk 😐

Sharmila: ok. I won't forward the finance thing

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel watching the story change, and why?
qa.a: Chandrika grew uneasy as 'someone had an upset stomach' became 'old meat' in a day, with nobody able to say who first said it.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do that stopped the rumour?
qa.a: Asked who first said it, got the kitchen inspection report from admin, and posted it in both groups.

qa.q: What was that day like for Ravi bhaiya?
qa.a: Ravi bhaiya, after eight years in the kitchen, looked shaky at lunch while nobody touched the chicken, harmed before any facts came out.

grounding: Shows a colleague watching an office rumour about the canteen cook grow with each group, and stopping it by asking who first said it.

passage: On Monday, at the handpump, Seema heard it first: Hemant, the new compounder at the health sub-centre, was keeping some of the free medicines. By Wednesday, on the temple steps, it had grown: he sold them in town. By Friday, in the women's group, someone said he had been caught, and a mother said she would not take her child to him anymore. Seema, who taught at the village primary school, had seen Hemant carry medicines on his cycle to houses in the rain. She asked each person the same question: "Who told you?" Each named someone else. Nobody had seen anything. On Saturday she walked to the sub-centre. Hemant's eyes were red. "Two families didn't bring their babies for vaccination this week," he said quietly. "Nobody has even asked me." Seema sat down. "Then let's ask the ANM to show the stock register at the panchayat meeting, in front of everyone."

qa.q: What had the rumour grown into by Wednesday?
qa.a: That Hemant sold the medicines in town.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling as the rumour grew?
qa.a: Seema felt uneasy and doubtful, remembering Hemant carrying medicines in the rain, and troubled that nobody had seen anything.

qa.q: What makes Seema's next step wise?
qa.a: Showing the stock register at the panchayat meeting tests the rumour with facts, in front of the same people who spread it.

qa.q: How has the rumour affected Hemant and the village?
qa.a: Hemant is hurt, his eyes red, and two families skipped their babies' vaccinations, so harm came before anyone asked who first said it.

grounding: Shows a neighbour watching a rumour about a health worker grow from group to group and cause harm before anyone asks who first said it.
